Pool of Bethesda
pool uv beth-EZ-duh
proper noun (place)
From Aramaic/Hebrew, possibly Beth-chesda ("house of mercy") or Beth-zatha; a pool in Jerusalem near the sheep market/gate, with five porches (John 5:2), where the Lord Jesus healed a man infirm for thirty-eight years.

Biblical Definition

The Pool of Bethesda (possibly "house of mercy") was a pool in Jerusalem near the sheep gate, surrounded by five porches, where a multitude of sick, blind, lame, and withered people lay, and where the Lord Jesus healed a man who had been infirm for thirty-eight years. John records: "Now there is at Jerusalem by the sheep market a pool, which is called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda, having five porches. In these lay a great multitude of impotent folk, of blind, halt, withered" (John 5:2-3). A man was there who had suffered his infirmity thirty-eight years — longer, perhaps, than many of those around him had been alive. The Lord saw him, knew his long-standing case, and asked the searching question, "Wilt thou be made whole?" (John 5:6). The man, fixated on the pool's waters and his inability to reach them in time, did not answer with faith but with his helplessness; yet the Lord, by sovereign grace, healed him with a word: "Rise, take up thy bed, and walk. And immediately the man was made whole, and took up his bed, and walked" (John 5:8-9). The healing took place on the Sabbath, provoking controversy with the Jewish leaders, who objected to the man carrying his bed; this led to the Lord's great discourse on His unity and equal working with the Father (John 5:17-47). The Pool of Bethesda teaches several lessons: the sovereignty of Christ's grace, which singled out one man from a multitude and healed him without his asking, on the ground of mercy alone (the "house of mercy" indeed); the helplessness of the sinner, pictured in the man who could not reach the healing waters by his own effort; and the power of Christ's word, which did in an instant what thirty-eight years of waiting by the pool could not do. The man's later warning from the Lord — "sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee" (John 5:14) — adds the sober note that physical healing is not the deepest need, and that the soul healed must turn from sin. Bethesda, the house of mercy, displays the mercy of Christ who heals the helpless by His sovereign word.

Webster 1828 Definition

A pool in Jerusalem near the sheep gate, with five porches, where multitudes of the sick lay, and where the Lord Jesus healed a man infirm 38 years with a word, by sovereign mercy (John 5:1-9); a picture of the helpless sinner healed by Christ's grace, with the warning "sin no more" (John 5:14).

POOL OF BETHESDA, proper noun. Possibly Beth-chesda ("house of mercy"); a pool in Jerusalem near the sheep gate, with five porches (John 5:2).

Where a multitude of the sick, blind, lame, and withered lay (John 5:3).

Where the Lord healed a man infirm for thirty-eight years, asking, "Wilt thou be made whole?" (John 5:6).

"Rise, take up thy bed, and walk" — healed by Christ's word, by sovereign mercy, without faith first asked (John 5:8-9).

The Sabbath healing provoked controversy and the Lord's discourse on His unity with the Father (John 5:17-47); the warning "sin no more" (John 5:14).

Key Scripture

John 5:5-6 — "And a certain man was there, which had an infirmity thirty and eight years. When Jesus saw him lie, and knew that he had been now a long time in that case, he saith unto him, Wilt thou be made whole?"

John 5:8-9 — "Jesus saith unto him, Rise, take up thy bed, and walk. And immediately the man was made whole, and took up his bed, and walked: and on the same day was the sabbath."

John 5:14 — "Afterward Jesus findeth him in the temple, and said unto him, Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee."

John 5:17 — "But Jesus answered them, My Father worketh hitherto, and I work."

Modern Corruption

The Pool of Bethesda is corrupted when the healing is read as a reward for the man's faith (which he did not show), when the "troubling of the water" tradition is over-weighted, or when the warning "sin no more" is severed from the healing.

expand to see more

Sovereign-mercy missed. The healing at Bethesda is a striking display of the sovereignty of Christ's grace. The Lord singled out one man from a great multitude of the sick — not the most faithful, not one who asked, not one who even knew who Jesus was (John 5:13) — and healed him on the ground of mercy alone. The man's response to "Wilt thou be made whole?" was not a confession of faith but a recital of his helplessness; yet Christ healed him anyway, by His own initiative and word. Bethesda ("house of mercy") thus pictures the gospel of sovereign grace: Christ heals the helpless sinner who cannot heal himself, choosing whom He will, on the ground of mercy, not the sinner's prior worthiness or even his asking. The thirty-eight years of failed effort by the pool could not do what Christ's word did in an instant.

The Pool of Bethesda has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering, beyond the sovereign mercy of the healing, is the Lord's solemn follow-up: "Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee" (John 5:14). The physical healing, great as it was, was not the man's deepest need; a worse thing than thirty-eight years of infirmity awaited the unrepentant — the eternal judgment of sin. The Lord who healed his body warned him to turn from sin, lest a worse thing come. Bethesda thus teaches that Christ's temporal mercies are meant to lead to repentance, and that the soul not turned from sin faces a worse calamity than any bodily affliction. The house of mercy issues a call to holiness: made whole, sin no more.
